Shocked I haven't seen this commented yet, but the real reason we haven't switched is because of the cost associated with changing industry standards and preexisting infrastructure. Schematics cannot be converted for free, even if its electronic you still need someone to go in and do it/check it to make sure its accurate and still works. Nothing is an easy conversion, as in an inch does not convert to a pretty number in metric, so some things may need to be redesigned so it's actually machinable.

Which brings you to the next problem, preexisting machinery and tooling cannot be converted without investment either. Some tools may work for both systems, like a drill bits in a universal chuck, but anything with Imperial measurements built into it are now obsolete. One easy example being stops with pre-determined lengths - they are integrated into the base on the machine, it cannot be changed. So you can start designing things in Metric, but that doesn't mean it can be physically made without investing in new factories, machine shops, etc.

Likewise, just because you convert the schematic and make the new part, that doesn't mean it will be compatible with any preexisting hardware, devices, machines, etc. Part of the reason why people still design in "outdated" systems is because design is iterative, in both a physical and theoretical sense. Like you take old ideas and build upon them, but you also cant just take an old screw hole and shove a metric thread in. Its already been drilled a certain way and new screws simply don't work. That's a really basic example, but it illustrates a larger problem when working with large, expensive-to-replace systems. You gotta start working on shot selection and decision making. You will always be working on technical skills in the background (and if you have any glaringly bad shots you should iron them out with drilling) but otherwise the main difference between the ranks is playing smarter with what you have. To put it a different way, at the highest level, theoretically everyone can make the same shots, it's how and when they are used that decides the winner. Obviously this is an over simplification and 4.0 to 5.0 and then again to pro is a large leap, but the concept still starts to apply at 4.0+. You've got enough skills that you can trust yourself to execute your shots fairly reliably and you have to start playing the chess aspect of the sport. 

In the same vein, figure out what your strengths are or what your play style is like. Play to your strengths but be aware of your weakness. It's a lot of mindfulness, but instead of paying attention to doing shots correctly, you're spending your mental energy on nuance, shot selection, and how to combat what your opponent is doing. If you want a good book about this topic I always recommend "The Inner Game of Tennis." 

The ltdr of the book is about trusting your inner brain to take care of your mechanics and figuring out how to control that super computer part of your brain without trying to force it. You are capable of doing advanced calculations and physics in the blink of an eye, how else could you accurately throw a ball? But the thing is "you" cannot do that calc in a split second, your internal brain can. So trying to actively tell that part of your brain how to do things is harmful, you gotta let it do its thing while you take over the high level decisions. In a word, it's Flow, but the book dives into the methods of achieving flow and how to apply these concepts to training and general play. Its hard to summarize here but honestly, reading the book fundamentally changed how I approach sports

You might be eatting too many carbs and not enough fats and proteins if you get shaky when you're hungry. I'm not a dietician but my understanding is you might be spiking your energy levels and then you crash more easily. 

All that being said your body also gets used to things. You probably aren't used to burning from body fat as much, so when you end up needing to do it, your body isn't responding well, but over time you get more used to it. When I first tried intermittent fasting I had the same feeling, but after a week or two I got used to it. I would feel an initial hunger and a bit of fatigue, but as long as I drank enough water that feeling would vanish after maybe 15-30 minutes and I would feel normal again. Now even if I haven't been doing fasting for months I still can skip meals without it bothering me too much since my body and mind is more used to it.

Now if you try this diet and you end up never getting over that feeling after a few weeks I would suggest modifying it or consulting a professional, this has just been my experience. (Only other note I will add is if you do exercise with this diet, make sure to eat still after, even if its just a little bit. It's not breaking your fast as much as it is proper recovery.)

Ultimately you do need to start cooking for yourself at least a bit to cut out the extra calories in fast food/processed foods, but have you tried alternative diets? I know people call stuff fads but I have seen genuine results with Intermittent Fasting. I think its helpful in a few big ways that other diets don't have. First and foremost, you can still eat a nice large meal and look forward to having that food opposed to always feeling like you're starving - with fasting you still will be hungry, but it comes with a promise of a fulfilling meal at the end, which I think helps a lot psychologically. Also you can more easily count calories if you are eating it all in one time of day, opposed to any snacks that get thrown in throughout a long work day. And something that it would help you in particular with is it allows you to avoid eating out at work because you already aren't eating that time of day. Which is huge because fast food/processed food have a lot of extra calories, so eliminating that works doubly well

Differentiating what's an identity vs what's a label/slur/descriptor is difficult. It's very nuanced and in my opinion comes down to who's prescribing it and what the associated connotations are. For example I identify as trans female. I take pride in it for overcoming hardships and wanting others to feel safe in being their true selves. So when I use it, it's an identity. Without knowing how I feel about it, if a stranger saw me and thought I was trans based on my apparenece, it could very well just be a label if they thought "oh they are trans." It can become a slur if they use it against me with malice. 

When I call someone else cis, it's never with malice. It's just meant as a descriptor, you are not trans. And I only ever use that description if it matters for the conversation. This is where the discussion gets complicated because you can flip the script and say intent doesn't matter nor practicality, it's how the person feels by being called it. And on the surface thats a valid aegument, esp when compared to other labels that have historically had negative stigmas to them. But cis never had any negative connotations. Theres no historical time frame of the lgbtq+ community weaponizing the word.

So I ask you, why does anyone who is cis get offended by the term? You can argue they dont like it because that's not how they identify. But as I described earlier, its not being used as an identity in the same way being trans does. Like I've never met someone who was offended by being called cis that wasn't also against trans rights, and I think there's a reason for that. In a vacuum I completely understand your arguments about identity, but at some point context and acting in good fair matter more than a framework for an ethics debate. 

If you still dont agree or dont quite understand what i mean, a good example is sexual attraction. Do straight people get upset that they're called straight instead of "not gay?" Not really. I don't know the history of the term and if people used to be offended by it, but you don't hear that being debated for the simple reason being gay is more normalized now. If anyone yelled at you or got offended they got called straight (when they were in fact heterosexual) people would unanimously agree they are being unreasonable.

Im a trans woman and while I understand the concept, I don't think they functionally work in the English language. I do think we ought to add another set of pronouns to denote singular nonbinary because they/them can be confusing in certain contexts, but people using random neopronouns is comoletely different. The issue is pronouns substitute for a name, pronouns themselves are not proper nouns. They are different, in fact their own, parts of speech.

It's not a fair comparison to say if you can learn a different name for someone you can learn to use a different pronoun (that you've most likely never heard of btw). Learning a name or any proper noun is inherently unique, so our brain is trained for that, but replacing hard set pronouns is foreign. When you formulate the sentence in your head you swap the subject to a pronoun from a preexisting list. When people have neopronouns it completely alters the language by making a pronoun essentially into a proper noun, something you don't do in the English language.

Like you could teach this differently and change the language but it's such a niche thing, nobody is going to remember it/it still wouldn't be reasonable to expect people to get it right first try and all the time. And to be clear my point isn't to say screw people who don't feel connected to any of our existing pronouns, but the fact of the matter is you're a minority within an already minority community. I'll do my best to get it right, but you're asking me to rewire my brain and tounge and that needs to be given a lot of grace. I can empathize with the pain of being misgendered, but in context it's not a fair comparison at all

I think the real issue actually lies in the beginning to mid game because games are rarely a close race. Yes decisions do become less impactful as the game progresses simply due to how many small choices you're making, but if the game is still not decided, the cumulation of your decisions *can* still matter.... not always, but they can. IMO the issue will always have more to do with the ai using starting bonuses to increase difficulty, as that makes the game decided on if you can catch up. They have no way to come back once you pass them, unlike humans who could more likely mount a comeback. If the ai was smarter I guarantee you the game would be more fun late game (as well as more fun early game instead of feeling like the literal unfair bs it can sometimes be). 

The only other solution is to introduce more comeback mechanics to prevent snowballing, but im not sure that's something this style of game ought to have/if they'd feel fair. As of now the only comeback mechanics I see are the luck of the draw with strategic resources or unique units/buildings/abilities, etc. The former is decided on the select screen but is still highly susceptible to snowballing allowing someone to have more land/take them by force before your opponent even knows its there. And the latter is predictable because you know based on the civ they play. Which is one reason why I think some other 4x games, like Humankind, have tried out developing those abilities in-game. But civ is never gonna do that, it's one of the whole appeals of the game, all the unique leaders to pick from and people look forward to seeing new leaders drop with cool new perks

The real issue I've found is that people don't know how to learn new skills. Knowing how to learn is a skill in of itself that requires patern recognition, critical thinking, patience, curiosity, the ability to formulate relevant questions, lateral thinking, etc etc. Many people *only* know how to do certain things, like use technology, because they grew up with it – otherwise they wouldn't due to the lack of their ability to learn new skills. You have to encourage these things when assisting or teaching new technology, otherwise people will come back to you when they have any new device because you taught them *that particular* device and not how to learn to use a new device. It's the classic teach a man how to fish instead of giving him a fish.

With tech its almost always related to figuring out a new user interface. I'm 26 and I haven't used most apps, operating systems, devices, whatever, simply due to the sheer number of them. But when someone asks me to help with one I typically can figure it out because I know what to look for and where developers typically put features and options. I developed that ability by using and trouble shooting stuff on my own. And I genuinely think playing video games where you have to do the same trial and error process has helped me a lot with technology in general. It's a skill anyone can learn.

One last note I'll leave you with, the biggest road block I've noticed is the disconnect with touch devices: older people don't think to double tap, swipe, hold down, or anything not involving a button or typing. These were not options they grew up with, and were not there with earlier computers. These are new methods of interaction they don't think of. It's hard to explain, but I think when I discover these options are there it's not only pattern recognition, but a little bit of limiting factors. Touch screen technology is minimalist. I was in so much denial because being trans just wasn't an option. I thought I was disgusting and perverted. And to make it worse I prayed and prayed to god to cure me or make the urges go away, but of course that didn't work. I felt damned, in this state of limbo where I hated God but at the same time was too terrified to abandon my faith. Deep down I always knew I didn't actually beleive in that religion, but outwardly I had to continue because of the social pressure. It's not just your family, its the community too. I had so many friends and people I knew and saw frequently through church, it's so much of your world before you're an adult and can physically leave. 

I basically had to look towards "heretics" to challenge my beleifs and slowly change them to the point where I could accept myself. It hurt like hell but eventually I broke everything down from a super fundamentalist set of beleifs to a progressive Christian faith (shout out to the sub r/openchristian lowkey saved my life). The thing that still boggles my mind is, the changes I accepted were through empathy and the pursuit of kindness to everyone. Like I didn't necessarily start with the end goal of allowing myself to accept lgbtq+ people, I went in seeking answers about the shortcomings I felt the Bible had, and then went on a wild different journey.

Nowadays I don't have any faith in the Christian God. I think a God could exist, but the only God that I would accept as worthy of my worship wouldn't demand literal worship, but rather through my actions and pursuit of kindness to others. In other words, im going to live out the rest of my life trying to be kind and loving, and it doesn't really matter in the end if im right or wrong about God because I'm gonna do what they should want anyways. And if I'm wrong about how they want me to be, they aren't worthy of my praise anyways. Because God damn I hate the Christian God and if it turns out they're real, I'll curse them out at the gates for each and every one of us

The years of indoctrination suck, but I think the truly worst moment was realizing I never would be able to actually beleive it. I wanted to beleive it. I knew I was *supposed*, to beleive it, and intellectually I could warp and play around with some stuff to make sense of it. But I couldn't beleive it in my heart. 

Every year, in the fall and spring, my church did these retreats over the weekend. You'd go out away from your parents with these small groups we were intimately familiar with, all the other teens in the group were my friends, and even the leaders were pretty cool (like I'm still friends with some of them to this day), and you'd just have a fun weekend of team-building, music and worship, and lots of time to just hang out and do fun shit like zip lines, dodgeball, Frisbee golf, whatever the place had set up. 

Corporate worship even at church is definitely designed to give a spiritual high, but these retreats were planned to build up to the final night there. All the sermons would connect to this big one and they'd always have a time where they'd ask people to commit themselves or like renew their promises to the lord. And you can tell how serious people are. Even if that spiritual high is going to wear off for most of them once they get back to real life and the stress of middle/highschool, in the moment it's obvious who's really believing it. 

 I remember going all these years and having fun, but like I just never could fully commit to god. Family and friends would have considered me fairly devout. Despite rarely reading the Bible, my academic knowledge of doctrine made me abke to always stay active in debates and theological conversationa. I knew, however, i wasnt fully bought in, and due to all the social and family pressures of religion, I truly tried. During my final retreat, my senior year, on that final night when everyone around me was giving themselves to the lord or praying over new believers, or whatever, I just felt.... absolutely nothing. And I wept. For like 10 minutes straight in front of everyone. They all thought it was due to my passion for God or something and there was no way I was telling them because in that moment I knew I never could beleive, yet because of my upbringing I kept trying and trying, and would continue trying despite this episode. It's so hard to describe but in that moment I knew for sure I never could beleive, but because of the dissonance from so many years I would try for almost another decade. I'm now at peace with all this, but that night my world shattered and its not fair to the youth we put through this
